introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores how defendants accidentally extend their own limitation periods through written acknowledgments or part payments. It concludes with Section 27—the extraordinary provision where limitation destroys the actual right of ownership.

core_concepts.title: Effect of Acknowledgment in Writing (Section 18)
core_concepts.description:
How a dying claim gets resurrected.
- The Rule: Where, **before the expiration** of the prescribed period for a suit, an acknowledgment of liability is made **in writing** signed by the party against whom such right is claimed, a **fresh period of limitation shall be computed** from the time the acknowledgment was signed.
- Essential Conditions: (1) It must be in writing and signed. (2) It must admit a jural relationship/liability. (3) Crucially, it must be made BEFORE the original limitation period expires. (An acknowledgment made after the time has already expired cannot revive a dead claim under the Limitation Act).

core_concepts.title: Effect of Payment on Account of Debt (Section 19)
core_concepts.description: Where payment on account of a debt is made **before the expiration** of the prescribed period by the person liable to pay, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time the payment was made. (Like Section 18, it resets the clock to zero from the date of payment).

core_concepts.title: Effect of Fraud or Mistake (Section 17)
core_concepts.description:
Fraud unravels everything.
- The Rule: If a person is kept away from the knowledge of their right to sue due to the **fraud** of the defendant, or if a right is concealed by fraud, the period of limitation does NOT begin to run until the plaintiff discovers the fraud, or could have discovered it with reasonable diligence.

core_concepts.title: Acquisition of Ownership by Prescription (Section 27)
core_concepts.description:
The grand exception to the rule that 'Limitation bars remedy, not right'.
- The Rule: At the determination of the period hereby limited to any person for instituting a suit for possession of any property, **his right to such property shall be extinguished**.
- Adverse Possession: If someone (a trespasser) occupies your land continuously, peacefully, and hostilely to your title for **12 years** (the limitation period for recovering possession of private immovable property), your right to file a suit is barred. Because of Section 27, your actual *title/ownership* is simultaneously EXTINGUISHED, and the trespasser legally becomes the new owner.

important_entities.name: Acknowledgment of a Time-Barred Debt (Contract Act exception)
important_entities.key_fact: Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act.
important_entities.significance: If an acknowledgment is made *after* the limitation period has expired, Section 18 of the Limitation Act cannot help. HOWEVER, under Section 25(3) of the Indian Contract Act, a written and signed promise to pay a time-barred debt is a completely valid, new contract. The creditor can sue on this *new* promise.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will set this scenario: 'A owes B money. Limitation ends on Jan 1, 2024. On Feb 1, 2024, A writes a letter acknowledging the debt. Does this start a fresh period of limitation under Section 18?' **NO**. The acknowledgment was made *after* the expiration of the period. Section 18 strictly requires the acknowledgment to be made *before* the time expires.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember that both written admissions and part payments effectively reset the limitation stopwatch to zero, provided they occur before the deadline.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing the interplay of property rights and equity, you must highlight **Section 27** as the doctrine of 'Extinctive Prescription', proving that prolonged inaction legally transfers ownership to promote the productive use of land.
